title: Coolant Pump "A" Control Circuit/Open
plain: The computer is watching the coolant pump "A" control circuit and sees what looks like a broken or disconnected circuit. Some engines use an electric pump to move coolant through the engine, turbo or heater.

causes.name: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the electric coolant pump
Broken or chafed wire in the coolant pump "A" control circuit
Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the circuit

checks: Watch the temperature gauge and pull over if it climbs
Look over the connector and wiring for the coolant pump "A" control circuit, checking for damage, corrosion or a loose fit
Check power, ground and resistance of the part with a meter
Clear the code and see if it comes back
fix: Repair the wiring or connector if it is damaged; otherwise replace the electric coolant pump.

title: Coolant Pump "A" Control Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The computer is watching the coolant pump "A" control circuit and is getting a signal that does not make sense for current conditions. Some engines use an electric pump to move coolant through the engine, turbo or heater.

causes.name: Failing or sticking electric coolant pump
A real problem in the system the part works with
Wiring or connector with high resistance
Computer software that needs an update

checks: Watch the temperature gauge and pull over if it climbs
Check for other codes that point to the underlying problem
Compare the coolant pump "A" control circuit reading with expected values in live data
Inspect the wiring and connector
fix: Find out whether the electric coolant pump itself or the system it works with is at fault, then repair or replace as needed.

title: Coolant Pump "A" Control Circuit Low
plain: The computer is watching the coolant pump "A" control circuit and is reading a voltage that is lower than it should be, which often means a short to ground or a failed part. Some engines use an electric pump to move coolant through the engine, turbo or heater.

causes.name: Control wire to the electric coolant pump shorted to ground

checks: Watch the temperature gauge and pull over if it climbs
Inspect the wiring in the coolant pump "A" control circuit for rubbed-through insulation touching metal
Check the wiring for a short to ground with a meter
Clear the code and see if it returns right away
fix: Fix any shorted wiring first; if the wiring tests good, replace the electric coolant pump.

title: Coolant Pump "A" Control Circuit High
plain: The computer is watching the coolant pump "A" control circuit and is reading a voltage that is higher than it should be, which often means a broken ground or a short to power. Some engines use an electric pump to move coolant through the engine, turbo or heater.

causes.name: Control wire to the electric coolant pump shorted to voltage or the part open inside

checks: Watch the temperature gauge and pull over if it climbs
Inspect the wiring and ground connection for the coolant pump "A" control circuit
Check for wires melted or rubbed together in the harness
Measure the circuit with a meter before replacing parts
fix: Repair the open ground or shorted wire; if the wiring is fine, replace the electric coolant pump.

title: Intake Air Heater System Performance
plain: The grid heater that warms incoming air on a diesel is not heating the way the computer expects. Cold starts may be harder.
symptoms: White smoke after a cold start

causes.name: Loose or corroded heater power cable

checks: Check the heater relay clicks on during a cold key-on
Measure heater element resistance and power cable connections
fix: Replace the failed relay or heater element and clean the power connections.

title: PTO Control Circuit/Open
plain: The computer is watching the PTO control circuit and sees what looks like a broken or disconnected circuit. The power take-off lets a work truck engine drive equipment like a pump or hoist.

causes.name: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the PTO control solenoid or relay
Broken or chafed wire in the PTO control circuit
Failed PTO control solenoid or relay
Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the circuit

checks: Look over the connector and wiring for the PTO control circuit, checking for damage, corrosion or a loose fit
Check power, ground and resistance of the part with a meter
Clear the code and see if it comes back
fix: Repair the wiring or connector if it is damaged; otherwise replace the PTO control solenoid or relay.

title: PTO Engaged Lamp Control Circuit
plain: The circuit for the light that shows the power take-off is engaged has a fault. This is common on work trucks only.
symptoms: PTO engaged light may not work
checks: Check the indicator lamp
Inspect the lamp wiring and connector
fix: Replace the lamp or repair the wiring.

title: Diesel Particulate Filter Regeneration Lamp Control Circuit
plain: The circuit for the dash light that tells you the diesel particulate filter is cleaning itself has a fault.
symptoms: Particulate filter cleaning light may not come on

causes.name: Faulty indicator lamp or cluster circuit
Instrument cluster or engine computer fault

checks: Check whether the lamp lights during a bulb check at key-on
Inspect the wiring between the computer and cluster
fix: Repair the wiring or the indicator circuit in the instrument cluster.

title: Evaporative System Monitoring Processor Performance
plain: The part of the computer that checks the fuel vapor (EVAP) system for leaks while the car is off is not working correctly.
symptoms: No change in how the car drives

causes.name: Engine computer or EVAP monitoring module needs a software update
Weak battery or power interruption while parked

checks: Check for a software update from the maker
Test the battery and charging system
fix: Update the module software; replace the module only if the fault remains.

title: ECM/PCM Internal Engine Off Timer Performance
plain: The engine computer keeps a timer that counts how long the engine has been off. That timer does not agree with other clocks in the car, so some self-tests cannot run.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives
May not pass an emissions readiness check

causes.name: Engine computer software that needs an update
Poor power or ground connection at the engine computer
Fault in another module that shares time data

checks: Test the battery and clean the terminals
Check for a software update or service bulletin for the engine computer
Clear the code and see if it returns after a few drive cycles
fix: Often fixed by a software update or by correcting a battery or power problem; the computer is rarely replaced.

causes.name: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at the A/C refrigerant distribution valve

checks: Look over the connector and wiring for the A/C refrigerant distribution valve control circuit, checking for damage, corrosion or a loose fit
Check power, ground and resistance of the part with a meter
Clear the code and see if it comes back
fix: Repair the wiring or connector if it is damaged; otherwise replace the A/C refrigerant distribution valve.

title: Camshaft Position Signal Output Circuit/Open
plain: The computer is watching the camshaft position signal output circuit and sees what looks like a broken or disconnected circuit. The engine computer passes the camshaft position signal on to another module, and that output line has a fault.
symptoms: Possible shifting, idle or gauge problems on systems that use the signal

causes.name: Wiring or connector fault between the engine computer and the module receiving the signal

checks: Look over the connector and wiring for the camshaft position signal output circuit, checking for damage, corrosion or a loose fit
Check power, ground and signal with a meter
Clear the code and see if it comes back
fix: Repair the wiring or connector; module replacement is only needed if the circuit tests good.
